title: Ukrainian literature and poetry
objectives: I can read the first stanza of the poem 'Запові́т' by Shevchenko with a word-for-word gloss and say what the poet asks for.
I can recognize poetic word order, with the adjective after the noun and the verb at the end of the line, and restate a poetic line in everyday order.
I can recognize the vocative when a poem speaks to the country, a river, the wind, fate or the poet's own thoughts ('Украї́но', 'Дні́пре', 'ві́тре', 'до́ле', 'ду́ми').
I can recognize older and poetic forms such as 'Вкраї́на', 'я́сная' and 'завива́' and give the everyday form of each, without using them in my own sentences.
I can talk about writers and their works, about poems, lines, rhymes and images, and about freedom and fate in classic Ukrainian literature.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ві́рша'. It names one poem; the plural 'ві́рші' also means verse in general, as in 'писа́ти ві́рші', to write poetry.

example.target: Сем чита́є вірш Шевче́нка про Дніпро́.
example.source: Sam is reading a poem by Shevchenko about the Dnipro.
example.source_literal: Sam reads poem of-Shevchenko about Dnipro.

vocabulary.note: Poetry as an art, or all the poems of a writer or a country: 'украї́нська пое́зія'. One poem is 'вірш'.
Genitive 'пое́та'. A man who writes poetry. A woman who writes poetry is 'пое́тка'.

example.source: Taras Shevchenko was a great poet.

vocabulary.note: The feminine of 'пое́т', built with the suffix '-ка', as 'а́вторка' is built from 'а́втор'. It is the usual word for a woman who writes poetry today; the older 'поете́са', with the suffix '-еса', is also standard.

example.target: Ця пое́тка пи́ше ві́рші про мо́ре.
example.source: This poet writes poems about the sea.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'рядка́'. The 'о' drops and the stress moves to the ending in every other form: 'у рядку́', 'рядки́', 'рядкі́в'. It is a line of a poem or of any written text.

example.target: Я пам’ята́ю пе́рший рядо́к цього́ ві́рша.
example.source: I remember the first line of this poem.

vocabulary.note: The same sound at the ends of two lines of verse.

example.target: У цих рядка́х ду́же га́рна ри́ма.
example.source: These lines have a very nice rhyme.
example.source_literal: In these lines very nice rhyme.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'о́бразу'. A picture that words create in the reader's mind; also a character in a book seen as a type, as in 'о́браз ма́тері', the figure of the mother.

example.target: Для пое́та Дніпро́ був о́бразом Украї́ни.
example.source: For the poet, the Dnipro was an image of Ukraine.
example.source_literal: For poet Dnipro was by-image of-Ukraine.

vocabulary.note: A noun in '-ння' from the verb 'оповіда́ти', to tell, a synonym of 'розповіда́ти'. The plural has the same form, and the genitive plural is 'оповіда́нь'.

example.source: Taras is writing a short story.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'рома́ну'. The man's name 'Рома́н' has the same spelling, but its genitive is 'Рома́на'.

example.target: Окса́на чита́є цей рома́н уже́ ти́ждень.
example.source: Oksana has been reading this novel for a week now.
example.source_literal: Oksana reads this novel already week.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'кобзаря́', plural 'кобзарі́'. 'Ко́бза' is a string instrument, and the culture note describes the kobzars. With a capital, 'Кобза́р' is the title of Shevchenko's first collection of poems, and Ukrainians often call the poet himself so.

example.target: Кобза́р ходи́в від села́ до села́ й співа́в.
example.source: The kobzar went from village to village and sang.

vocabulary.note: Two meanings: a long epic song of the kobzars, and, in older and poetic language, a thought. The everyday word for a thought is 'ду́мка'.

example.source: The kobzars sang long epic songs.

vocabulary.note: A noun in '-ння', like 'оповіда́ння'. After 'шука́ти' and 'чека́ти' it usually stands in the genitive, as other abstract nouns do.

example.source: Where do poets look for inspiration?

vocabulary.note: Two meanings: freedom, especially the freedom of a people, and will, a person's wish or decision. 'На во́лі' means 'in freedom'.

example.target: Ко́жна люди́на хо́че жи́ти на во́лі.
example.source: Every person wants to live in freedom.
example.source_literal: Every person wants to-live on freedom.

vocabulary.note: The course a life takes, and a person's lot, the share of good and bad that life gives. Folk songs and poems speak to it as to a person.
Genitive 'ві́тру': the 'е' drops when an ending is added.
Genitive 'сте́пу', locative 'у степу́', with the stress on the ending. The steppe is wide grassland without trees; it covers the south and east of Ukraine.

example.source: We drove across the steppe for a long time.

vocabulary.note: A grave; in the steppe also a burial mound, an old earthen hill raised over a grave.

example.source: Shevchenko's grave stands above the Dnipro.

dialogues.title: Four lines about the Dnipro
dialogues.context: In class, Iryna Petrivna gives Sam the four lines that open a long poem by Shevchenko and describe a stormy night on the Dnipro. 'Вго́лос' means aloud, 'запам’ята́ти' is to memorize, and 'у кінці́' means at the end. 'Фо́рма' is a form. 'Біль' is pain, genitive 'бо́лю'. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, прочита́йте, будь ла́ска, ці чоти́ри рядки́ вго́лос.
lines.source: Sam, please read these four lines aloud.
lines.source_literal: Sam, read, please, these four lines aloud.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: «Реве́ та сто́гне Дніпр широ́кий, серди́тий ві́тер завива́, додо́лу ве́рби гне висо́кі, гора́ми хви́лі підійма́.»
lines.source: 'The wide Dnipro roars and groans, the angry wind howls, it bends the tall willows to the ground, it raises the waves like mountains.'
lines.source_literal: 'Roars and groans Dnipro wide, angry wind howls, down-to-ground willows bends tall, by-mountains waves raises.'

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. Що ви ба́чите, коли́ чита́єте ці рядки́?
lines.source: Very good. What do you see when you read these lines?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я ба́чу ніч на Дніпрі́. Ві́тер гне ве́рби, а хви́лі вели́кі, як го́ри.
lines.source: I see a night on the Dnipro. The wind is bending the willows, and the waves are as big as mountains.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так. А як ви ду́маєте, чому́ рі́чка реве́ й сто́гне?
lines.source: Yes. And why do you think the river roars and groans?
lines.source_literal: Yes. And how you think, why river roars and groans?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ здає́ться, що пое́т ба́чить у Дніпрі́ люди́ну, яка́ сто́гне від бо́лю.
lines.source: It seems to me that the poet sees in the Dnipro a person groaning with pain.
lines.source_literal: To-me seems, that poet sees in Dnipro person, who groans from pain.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Са́ме так. Ось що таке́ о́браз: пое́т малю́є слова́ми, а ми ба́чимо ніч, ві́тер і рі́чку.
lines.source: Exactly. That is what an image is: the poet paints with words, and we see the night, the wind and the river.
lines.source_literal: Exactly so. Here what such image: poet paints by-words, and we see night, wind and river.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А чому́ тут «Дніпр», а не «Дніпро́»? І чому́ «завива́», а не «завива́є»?
lines.source: And why is it 'Дніпр' here and not 'Дніпро́'? And why 'завива́' and not 'завива́є'?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Це старі́ фо́рми, які́ ча́сто є в пое́зії. Так пое́т ро́бить рядо́к коро́тшим.
lines.source: These are old forms that are common in poetry. That way the poet makes the line shorter.
lines.source_literal: These old forms, which often there-are in poetry. So poet makes line by-shorter.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А ще ми ка́жемо «широ́кий Дніпро́», а тут «Дніпр широ́кий».
lines.source: And we say 'широ́кий Дніпро́', but here it's 'Дніпр широ́кий'.
lines.source_literal: And also we say 'wide Dnipro', and here 'Dnipr wide'.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, у пое́зії слова́ ча́сто стоя́ть іна́кше, ніж у розмо́ві. Прикме́тник іде́ пі́сля іме́нника, а дієсло́во стої́ть у кінці́ рядка́.
lines.source: Yes, in poetry words often stand in a different order than in conversation. The adjective comes after the noun, and the verb stands at the end of the line.
lines.source_literal: Yes, in poetry words often stand otherwise, than in conversation. Adjective goes after noun, and verb stands in end of-line.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ найбі́льше подо́бається о́браз серди́того ві́тру.
lines.source: I like the image of the angry wind best.
lines.source_literal: To-me most pleases image of-angry of-wind.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Тоді́ до насту́пного уро́ку запам’ята́йте ці чоти́ри рядки́.
lines.source: Then memorize these four lines by the next lesson.
lines.source_literal: Then until next lesson memorize these four lines.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Запам’ята́ю, Іри́но Петрі́вно. З ри́мою це не ду́же ва́жко.
lines.source: I will, Iryna Petrivna. With the rhyme it isn't very hard.
lines.source_literal: I-will-memorize, Iryna Petrivna. With rhyme this not very hard.

dialogues.title: Books from school
dialogues.context: Sam has asked Oksana what to read in Ukrainian. At Andrii's café she and Taras remember the books they read at school. 'Літерату́ра' is literature, and Mavka, a girl of the forest, is the heroine of Lesia Ukrainka's play 'The Forest Song'. They are friends and say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Тара́се, Сем хо́че почита́ти украї́нську літерату́ру. Що йому́ пора́дити?
lines.source: Taras, Sam wants to read some Ukrainian literature. What should we recommend to him?
lines.source_literal: Taras, Sam wants to-read Ukrainian literature. What to-him to-advise?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Дава́й почнемо́ з того́, що ми чита́ли в шко́лі. Ти пам’ята́єш «Лісову́ пі́сню» Ле́сі Украї́нки?
lines.source: Let's start with what we read at school. Do you remember 'The Forest Song' by Lesia Ukrainka?
lines.source_literal: Let's we-will-start from that, what we read in school. You remember 'Forest Song' of-Lesia Ukrainka?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Звича́йно. Я ду́же люби́ла Ма́вку, і мені́ було́ шко́да, що в не́ї така́ до́ля.
lines.source: Of course. I loved Mavka very much, and I was sorry that she had such a fate.
lines.source_literal: Of-course. I very loved Mavka, and to-me was pity, that at her such fate.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А мені́ бі́льше подо́балися рома́ни. Рома́н Іва́на Багря́ного «Тигроло́ви» я прочита́в за три дні.
lines.source: And I liked novels more. I read Ivan Bahrianyi's novel 'The Tiger Hunters' in three days.
lines.source_literal: And to-me more pleased novels. Novel of-Ivan of-Bahrianyi 'Tiger-catchers' I read within three days.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А я до́вгі рома́ни не люби́ла. Мені́ бі́льше подо́балися оповіда́ння, бо їх мо́жна прочита́ти за оди́н ве́чір.
lines.source: And I didn't like long novels. I liked short stories better, because you can read them in one evening.
lines.source_literal: And I long novels not loved. To-me more pleased short-stories, because them possible to-read within one evening.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Напри́клад, оповіда́ння Франка́ про хло́пчика в шко́лі? Я його́ й тепе́р пам’ята́ю.
lines.source: Like Franko's short story about a little boy at school? I still remember it.
lines.source_literal: For-example, short-story of-Franko about little-boy in school? I it also now remember.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так. А ще ми запам’ята́ли «Запові́т». Його́ я зна́ю й сього́дні: «Як умру́, то похова́йте мене́ на моги́лі».
lines.source: Yes. And we also memorized 'The Testament'. I still know it today: 'When I die, bury me on a burial mound'.
lines.source_literal: Yes. And also we memorized 'Testament'. It I know also today: 'When I-will-die, then bury me on grave'.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тоді́ я ду́мав, що цей вірш ті́льки про моги́лу. А тепе́р розумі́ю, що він про во́лю.
lines.source: Back then I thought this poem was only about a grave. But now I understand that it's about freedom.
lines.source_literal: Then I thought, that this poem only about grave. And now understand, that it about freedom.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так. Пое́т хоті́в, щоб украї́нці ста́ли ві́льними.
lines.source: Yes. The poet wanted Ukrainians to become free.
lines.source_literal: Yes. Poet wanted, so-that Ukrainians became by-free.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А ти зна́єш, чому́ Шевче́нка зва́ли Кобзаре́м?
lines.source: And do you know why Shevchenko was called the Kobzar?
lines.source_literal: And you know, why Shevchenko they-called by-Kobzar?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Бо його́ пе́ршою кни́гою був «Кобза́р».
lines.source: Because his first book was 'Kobzar'.
lines.source_literal: Because his by-first by-book was 'Kobzar'.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: І ще тому́, що він, як кобзарі́, співа́в про во́лю й до́лю Украї́ни.
lines.source: And also because, like the kobzars, he sang of the freedom and the fate of Ukraine.
lines.source_literal: And also for-that-reason that he, like kobzars, sang about freedom and fate of-Ukraine.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: То що ми пора́димо Се́мові?
lines.source: So what shall we recommend to Sam?
lines.source_literal: So what we will-advise to-Sam?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Споча́тку оповіда́ння Франка́, а по́тім «Лісову́ пі́сню». А ві́рші хай чита́є з Іри́ною Петрі́вною.
lines.source: First Franko's short stories, and then 'The Forest Song'. And he can read the poems with Iryna Petrivna.
lines.source_literal: First short-stories of-Franko, and then 'Forest Song'. And poems let reads with Iryna Petrivna.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: рядо́к, ві́тер, кобза́р and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
The new words of this unit are read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss.

'Рядо́к' and 'ві́тер' lose a vowel in their other forms: 'рядо́к', 'рядка́'; 'ві́тер', 'ві́тру'. Such a vowel is called a fleeting vowel: it stands in the last syllable of the nominative, which ends in a consonant, and it disappears when an ending adds a syllable, as in 'кіт', 'кота́'. In 'рядо́к' the 'я' shows that the 'р' is soft, and the stress moves to the ending in every other form: 'у рядку́', 'рядки́'.

'Степ' keeps its vowel but moves its stress: 'сте́пу' in the genitive, but 'у степу́' in the locative. 'Вірш' has one syllable and so no mark; its other forms are stressed on the stem: 'ві́рша', 'у ві́рші', 'ві́рші'.

'Кобза́р' ends in a hard [r], because 'р' at the end of a word is always hard, but its stem is soft, and the softness shows in every form with an ending: 'кобзаря́', 'кобзарі́', and the vocative 'кобзарю́'. The stress moves to the ending in all of them.

'Пое́т', 'пое́тка' and 'пое́зія' have two vowels side by side, 'о' and 'е', and each is said in full: [pɔˈɛt]. In 'пое́зія' the 'з' is soft before 'і', and the 'я' after the vowel 'і' is [jɑ]: [pɔˈɛzʲijɑ].

'На́тхнення' and 'оповіда́ння' end in '-ння', the doubled consonant of nouns made from verbs: one long soft [nʲː]. In 'на́тхнення' the 'т' and the 'х' are said one after the other, [tx], with no vowel between them. 'Во́ля' and 'до́ля' have a soft 'л' before 'я'. 'О́браз' ends in a voiced [z], since voiced consonants keep their voice at the end of a word, and 'моги́ла' has the [ɦ] of 'г'. 'Ду́ма', 'ри́ма' and 'рома́н' are spelled as they are said.

'П’є́са', a play, and 'запам’ята́ти', to memorize, have the apostrophe: the 'п' and the 'м' before it stay hard, and the 'є' and the 'я' after it are said with [j], [ˈpjɛsɑ] and [zɑpɑmjɑˈtɑtɪ]. In 'вго́лос', aloud, the 'в' stands before a consonant and is said [w]. In 'Ге́тьте', away, the soft sign makes the first 'т' soft before the hard second one: [ˈɦɛtʲtɛ]. 'Дніпро́' moves its stress to the first syllable in the vocative 'Дні́пре'.

Classic poems also use spellings that the learner reads but does not write. 'Вкраї́на' is a poetic variant of 'Украї́на': poets use it after a word that ends in a vowel, where 'у' would put two vowels side by side, by the same euphony that chooses between 'у' and 'в' as a preposition. Its 'в' stands before a consonant and is said [w]. Today the name is always written 'Украї́на'. The uncontracted adjective endings, such as 'я́сная' for 'я́сна' and 'си́нєє' for 'си́нє', add one syllable: 'я́сная' has three syllables, [ˈjɑsnɑjɑ], and the 'є' of 'си́нєє' shows the soft 'н' of the stem 'син-'. The note on older forms explains them.

examples.source: There is no rhyme in the second line.

examples.target: Без ві́тру в степу́ ду́же ти́хо.
examples.source: Without wind it is very quiet in the steppe.
examples.source_literal: Without of-wind in steppe very quiet.

examples.source: The whole village listened to the kobzar's songs.
Lesia Ukrainka's poetry is very rich.
We had a rest in the steppe.

grammar.title: Talking about literature: вірш, рядо́к, ри́ма, о́браз
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian talks about books with a few patterns that join known cases to the new nouns.

- The author follows the work in the genitive: 'вірш Шевче́нка', a poem by Shevchenko, literally 'poem of-Shevchenko'; 'рома́н Франка́', a novel by Franko.
- The topic of a work follows 'про' with the accusative: 'вірш про во́лю', a poem about freedom.
- A place in a work takes 'у' or 'в' with the locative: 'у ві́рші', 'в рома́ні', 'в оповіда́нні', 'у пе́ршому рядку́'.
- The author takes the instrumental after a passive participle: 'вірш, напи́саний Шевче́нком', a poem written by Shevchenko.
- A writer's role takes the instrumental after 'бу́ти' in the past: 'Вона́ була́ пое́ткою.'

The words for kinds of text name what each one is:

- 'Вірш' is one poem, a text in lines with a regular rhythm. Rhythm is the repeated pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.
- 'Пое́зія' is poetry as an art, or all the poems of a writer or a country: 'пое́зія Ле́сі Украї́нки'.
- 'Рядо́к' is one line of a poem or of any text.
- 'Ри́ма' is the same sound at the ends of two lines: in 'Запові́т', 'моги́лі' rhymes with 'ми́лій'.
- 'О́браз' is an image, a picture that words create, such as the angry wind in Shevchenko's lines about the Dnipro. The same word names a character in a book seen as a type: 'о́браз ма́тері', the figure of the mother.
- 'Оповіда́ння' is a short story, which can be read at one sitting, and 'рома́н' is a novel, a long story in prose. Prose is ordinary language, not divided into lines of verse.
- 'Ду́ма' is an epic song of the kobzars and, in older and poetic language, a thought.
- 'П’є́са' is a play, a work written to be performed on the stage.

The people who write have masculine and feminine names. 'Пое́т' and 'пое́тка' are a man and a woman who write poetry; 'письме́нник' is a writer, and a woman writer is 'письме́нниця', with the suffix '-иця'; 'а́втор' and 'а́вторка' are the man and the woman who wrote a given work. The current spelling rules give these feminine forms as standard.

examples.source_literal: This poem of-Lesia Ukrainka about hope.

examples.target: У цьо́му оповіда́нні є ціка́вий о́браз ма́тері.

examples.source_literal: In this short-story there-is interesting image of-mother.

grammar.title: Poetic word order: the adjective after the noun, the verb at the end
grammar.explanation:
In Ukrainian the endings, not the position of a word, show who does what: the subject is in the nominative, the object in the accusative, and an adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. Word order is therefore free to carry emphasis, and poetry uses this freedom for the rhythm of the line and for the rhyme at its end.

In everyday speech and in prose the neutral order is this:

- An adjective stands before its noun: 'широ́кий степ', the wide steppe.
- The subject comes first, then the verb, then the object: 'Ві́тер гне ве́рби.', the wind bends the willows.

In poetry both rules are often reversed:

- The adjective follows the noun: 'Дніпр широ́кий' for 'широ́кий Дніпро́', and 'се́ред сте́пу широ́кого' for 'се́ред широ́кого сте́пу', amid the wide steppe.
- The verb goes to the end of the line, where the rhyme falls: 'Гора́ми хви́лі підійма́.', it raises the waves like mountains.
- An adjective can even be separated from its noun by the verb: in 'Додо́лу ве́рби гне висо́кі.' the adjective 'висо́кі' belongs to 'ве́рби', and its plural ending shows it.

To read such a line, find the verb first, then its subject, then attach each adjective to the noun whose gender, number and case it shares. Where the nominative and the accusative look the same, agreement and meaning decide: in 'Додо́лу ве́рби гне висо́кі.' the verb 'гне' is singular, so the plural 'ве́рби' cannot be its subject. The one who bends is the wind of the line before, and 'ве́рби' is the object.

The examples are the four lines that open a long poem by Taras Shevchenko and describe a stormy night on the Dnipro; Ukrainians also know them as a song. They use these words:

- 'реві́ти', to roar, with 'реве́', it roars
- 'стогна́ти', to groan, with 'сто́гне', it groans
- 'широ́кий', wide
- 'серди́тий', angry
- 'завива́ти', to howl
- 'додо́лу', down to the ground
- 'ве́рба', willow
- 'гну́ти', to bend, with 'гне', it bends
- 'хви́ля', wave
- 'підійма́ти', to raise

'Дніпр' and the verb forms 'завива́' and 'підійма́' are older poetic forms, explained in the note on older forms. 'Гора́ми' is the instrumental plural of 'гора́', mountain, used for likeness: 'like mountains'. This use of the instrumental belongs mainly to poetry and folk song; everyday speech says 'як го́ри'.

The learner's own sentences keep the neutral order. Restating a poetic line in that order, as the last example does, is the best way to check that one has understood it.

rows: The wind bends the tall willows.

examples.source: The wide Dnipro roars and groans.
The angry wind howls.
It bends the tall willows to the ground.
It raises the waves like mountains.

examples.target: Серди́тий ві́тер гне висо́кі ве́рби додо́лу й підійма́є хви́лі, як го́ри.
examples.source: The angry wind bends the tall willows to the ground and raises waves like mountains.
examples.source_literal: Angry wind bends tall willows down-to-ground and raises waves, like mountains.

grammar.title: The vocative in poetry: Украї́но, Дні́пре, до́ле
grammar.explanation:
The vocative is the case of address, the form of a noun used to call or speak to someone: 'Окса́но', 'Тара́се', 'Іри́но Петрі́вно'. Poetry extends it to things that cannot hear. A poet speaks to the country, to a river, to the wind, to fate or to his own thoughts as if each were a person. This device is called personification, giving a thing the qualities of a person, and the vocative is its grammatical sign. In a poem, a noun in the vocative tells the reader who or what is being spoken to.

The endings are the ones of the unit on greetings:

- A feminine noun in '-а' takes '-о': 'Украї́на', 'Украї́но'; 'ду́ма', 'ду́мо'.
- A feminine noun in '-я' after a consonant takes '-е': 'до́ля', 'до́ле'; 'во́ля', 'во́ле'; 'пі́сня', 'пі́сне'.
- A masculine noun with a hard stem takes '-е': 'пое́т', 'пое́те'. A fleeting vowel drops before it: 'ві́тер', 'ві́тре'. 'Дніпро́' also takes '-е', and its stress moves to the first syllable: 'Дні́пре'.
- A masculine noun with a soft stem takes '-ю': 'кобза́р', 'кобзарю́'.
- In the plural the vocative has the form of the nominative: 'ду́ми'.

An adjective or a possessive pronoun beside a vocative keeps its nominative form, as in 'Шано́вний па́не', and in poetry it usually follows the noun: 'ду́ми мої́', my thoughts; 'Дні́пре широ́кий', wide Dnipro. The interjections 'о' and 'ой' often come before the address, much as an English poem says 'O', and 'ой' opens many folk songs.

Two famous openings show the device:

- A poem in the collection 'Кобза́р' begins 'Ду́ми мої́, ду́ми мої́, ли́хо мені́ з ва́ми!' The poet speaks to his own thoughts. 'Ли́хо' is woe or misfortune, and 'ли́хо мені́ з ва́ми' is literally 'woe to-me with you'.
- Lesia Ukrainka begins her poem 'Contra spem spero', a Latin title meaning 'I hope against hope', with 'Ге́тьте, ду́ми, ви хма́ри осі́нні!' 'Ге́тьте' is the word 'геть', away, with the ending '-те' of a command to more than one person, and 'хма́ри' are clouds: her gloomy thoughts are autumn clouds that she sends away.

The same vocatives are used outside poetry, in songs, speeches and letters, wherever a speaker addresses the country or a river: 'Украї́но', 'Дні́пре'.

examples.target: Ду́ми мої́, ду́ми мої́, ли́хо мені́ з ва́ми!
examples.source: My thoughts, my thoughts, you bring me nothing but woe!
examples.source_literal: Thoughts my, thoughts my, woe to-me with you!

examples.source: Away, my thoughts, you autumn clouds!

examples.target: Дні́пре широ́кий, куди́ ти несе́ш свою́ во́ду?
examples.source: Wide Dnipro, where are you carrying your water?
examples.source_literal: Dnipro wide, where you carry own water?

examples.source: Wind, where are you flying?
Oh Ukraine, you are our hope.

grammar.title: Older and poetic forms, for recognition only
grammar.explanation:
Classic poems and folk songs keep forms that the modern standard language has replaced. A reader needs to recognize them and to know the everyday form behind each one, but they are never used in the learner's own sentences. Most of them give a line one syllable more or one syllable less than the everyday form would.

These are the forms met most often:

- 'Вкраї́на' for 'Украї́на', after a word that ends in a vowel: 'на Вкраї́ні ми́лій'.
- 'Дніпр' for 'Дніпро́', one syllable shorter.
- Uncontracted adjective endings: 'я́сная' for 'я́сна', 'си́нєє' for 'си́нє', 'молоді́ї' for 'молоді́'. They are the older full endings, from which the modern ones were contracted, and each adds one syllable.
- Verb forms of 'він' and 'вона́' without their final '-є': 'завива́' for 'завива́є', 'підійма́' for 'підійма́є'.

Other points concern words that are standard today but that classic poems use in ways everyday speech avoids, or with the meaning of their time:

- 'Як' can mean 'when' or 'if': 'Як умру́' means 'Коли́ я помру́', when I die. Speech also uses 'як' in this way, but careful writing prefers 'коли́' or 'якщо́'. 'Умру́' is the 'я' form of the perfective future of 'уме́рти', to die, a synonym of 'поме́рти'.
- An adjective can stand alone for a noun: in 'Запові́т', 'реву́чий', roaring, made from 'реві́ти' with the suffix '-уч-', names the roaring river. Everyday speech names the thing itself or says 'той, що реве́', the one that roars.
- '-сь' for '-ся' after a vowel, also in the infinitive: 'смія́тись' for 'смія́тися', to laugh, and 'сподіва́тись' for 'сподіва́тися'. It is a variant of the same suffix, correct in any text, and poetry uses it often because it is one syllable shorter.
- Shevchenko wrote 'на Вкраї́ні', with 'на', as was usual in his time. The standard today is 'в Украї́ні', and that is the only form for the learner's own sentences.
- In classic poetry 'во́ля' is above all the freedom of a people from serfdom and foreign rule, and 'до́ля' is fate as a power that a person meets, often spoken to as a person.

A well-known song with words by Mykhailo Starytsky opens with an uncontracted ending, 'Ніч яка́ мі́сячна, зо́ряна, я́сная!' 'Мі́сячний' is moonlit, from 'мі́сяць' in its meaning 'moon', and 'зо́ряний' is starry, from 'зоря́', star. In everyday words the line is 'Яка́ мі́сячна, зо́ряна, я́сна ніч!'

examples.source: What a moonlit, starry, bright night!
What a moonlit, starry, bright night!
To go on hoping, without hope.
Oh, you blue sea!

grammar.title: Reading 'Запові́т': the words of the first stanza
grammar.explanation:
'Запові́т' means testament: the last wishes a person leaves to those who live on. Shevchenko wrote the poem in December 1845, when he was seriously ill and thought that he would die. A stanza is a group of lines that forms one unit of a poem, and the first stanza of 'Запові́т' has eight lines. In the reading each paragraph holds two of them.

The stanza uses these words:

- 'то' opens the main clause after a clause with 'як' or 'якщо́', like English 'then'.
- 'похова́йте' is the plural command of the perfective verb 'похова́ти', to bury.
- 'се́ред', amid or in the middle of, is a preposition with the genitive.
- 'ми́лий' is dear or beloved.
- 'лани́' is the plural of 'лан', a wide field of grain.
- 'широкопо́лий', with wide fields, joins 'широ́кий', wide, and 'по́ле', field.
- 'кру́чі' is the plural of 'кру́ча', a steep high bank above a river.
- 'ви́дно' and 'чу́ти' are predicative words: 'ви́дно' means 'can be seen', and 'чу́ти', spelled like the infinitive 'to hear', means 'can be heard'.

'Як умру́', 'Вкраї́на', 'на Вкраї́ні' and 'реву́чий' are explained in the note on older forms. In the last line, 'як реве́ реву́чий', the word 'як' means 'how'.

The last four lines form one clause with 'щоб', so that. 'Було́ ви́дно, було́ чу́ти' is a sentence without a grammatical subject, the past of 'ви́дно' and 'чу́ти' with the neuter form 'було́'. 'Щоб' takes this past form, as it does after a wish. What can be seen, 'лани́', 'Дніпро́' and 'кру́чі', is the object, in the accusative, which for these nouns has the form of the nominative. In everyday words the clause says 'щоб із моги́ли було́ ви́дно поля́, Дніпро́ й кру́чі й було́ чу́ти, як реве́ Дніпро́'.

The stanza also shows the patterns of the earlier notes: the adjective after the noun in 'се́ред сте́пу широ́кого' and 'на Вкраї́ні ми́лій', and the rhyme of 'моги́лі' with 'ми́лій' and of 'кру́чі' with 'реву́чий'.

examples.source: An old burial mound stands amid the steppe.
From the steep bank you can see the whole Dnipro.
Here you can hear the wind roaring.
Shevchenko was buried above the Dnipro.

culture.title: Kobzars, dumy and the collection 'Кобза́р'
culture.text:
Before printed books reached the villages, much of Ukrainian poetry and history lived in song. The wandering singers called 'кобзарі́' were usually blind. A kobzar went from village to village and from fair to fair and sang to his own playing on a string instrument plucked with the fingers, either 'ко́бза' or 'банду́ра', which is larger. Kobzars formed brotherhoods with their own rules, and each took a boy as a guide, who led him on the road and learned the songs from him.

The great form of the kobzars was the epic song called 'ду́ма': a long song in lines of uneven length, without stanzas. Dumy tell of the Cossacks, the free communities of warriors who lived on the steppe from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century: of their battles, of captivity in foreign lands, of a Cossack dying alone in the steppe. The images of this unit come from that world:

- 'степ', the open steppe, a place of freedom and of danger
- 'моги́ла', the burial mound raised over a fallen warrior, which stands on the steppe for centuries
- 'ві́тер', the wind that carries news across the steppe
- 'во́ля', the freedom the Cossacks fought for
- 'до́ля', fate, which a song speaks to as to a person

In 1840 Taras Shevchenko published his first collection of poems and named it 'Кобза́р'. He was born in 1814 as a serf, a peasant who belonged to a landowner together with the land, and in 1838 friends who admired his talent as a painter bought his freedom. Because of his poems against serfdom and against the Russian Empire, which then ruled most of Ukraine, he was sent in 1847 to serve as a soldier at a distant post, forbidden to write and to draw, and he was released only in 1857. He died in 1861, and his friends brought him home and buried him on a hill above the Dnipro near Kaniv, as 'Запові́т' asks. Ukrainians often call him simply 'Кобза́р', and in many village homes his book was kept in a place of honor.

Every year around 9 March, Shevchenko's birthday, people read his poems at his monuments, and 'Запові́т', set to music, is sung at the end of many ceremonies.

Three writers of this unit appear on Ukrainian banknotes:

- Ivan Franko, a poet, novelist and scholar from Galicia, the region around Lviv, on the twenty-hryvnia note
- Taras Shevchenko on the hundred-hryvnia note
- Lesia Ukrainka on the two-hundred-hryvnia note

readings.title: The poem 'Запові́т' by Shevchenko: the first stanza

paragraphs.target: Шевче́нко написа́в «Запові́т» у гру́дні ти́сяча вісімсо́т со́рок п’я́того ро́ку, коли́ був ду́же хво́рий. Ось пе́рші ві́сім рядкі́в цього́ ві́рша.
paragraphs.source: Shevchenko wrote 'The Testament' in December 1845, when he was very ill. Here are the first eight lines of the poem.
paragraphs.source_literal: Shevchenko wrote 'Testament' in December thousand eight-hundred forty of-fifth of-year, when was very ill. Here first eight of-lines of-this of-poem.

paragraphs.target: Як умру́, то похова́йте мене́ на моги́лі,
paragraphs.source: When I die, bury me on a burial mound,
paragraphs.source_literal: When I-will-die, then bury me on grave,

paragraphs.target: Се́ред сте́пу широ́кого, на Вкраї́ні ми́лій,
paragraphs.source: amid the wide steppe, in beloved Ukraine,
paragraphs.source_literal: Amid of-steppe wide, on Ukraine dear,

paragraphs.target: Щоб лани́ широкопо́лі, і Дніпро́, і кру́чі
paragraphs.source: so that the broad fields, the Dnipro and its steep banks
paragraphs.source_literal: So-that fields wide-fielded, and Dnipro, and steep-banks

paragraphs.target: Було́ ви́дно, було́ чу́ти, як реве́ реву́чий.
paragraphs.source: are in sight, and I can hear the roaring river roar.
paragraphs.source_literal: Was visible, was audible, how roars roaring.

choices: In December 1845, when he was very ill
questions.explanation: 'Шевче́нко написа́в «Запові́т» у гру́дні ти́сяча вісімсо́т со́рок п’я́того ро́ку, коли́ був ду́же хво́рий.' The year is in the genitive after the month: in December of the year 1845.

questions.prompt: Where does the poet ask to be buried?
choices: By the sea, far from home
On a burial mound amid the wide steppe, in Ukraine
questions.explanation: 'Похова́йте мене́ на моги́лі, се́ред сте́пу широ́кого, на Вкраї́ні ми́лій': on a burial mound, amid the wide steppe, in beloved Ukraine.

questions.prompt: What does he want to see and hear from his grave?
choices: The fields, the Dnipro and its steep banks, and the roar of the river
The bells of the city and the voices of his friends
questions.explanation: 'Щоб лани́ широкопо́лі, і Дніпро́, і кру́чі було́ ви́дно, було́ чу́ти, як реве́ реву́чий.' The fields, the river and its banks should be in sight, and the river's roar should be heard.

questions.prompt: Who is 'реву́чий', the roaring one, in the last line?
questions.explanation: The Dnipro is named two lines earlier, and 'реве́' is the verb used for a river in a storm. 'Реву́чий' is an adjective made from 'реві́ти' and used here in place of a noun, a poetic device.

paragraphs.target: Ле́ся Украї́нка народи́лася в ти́сяча вісімсо́т сімдеся́т пе́ршому ро́ці на Воли́ні. Наспра́вді її́ зва́ли Лари́са Ко́сач, а Ле́сею її́ зва́ли вдо́ма. Свої́ ві́рші вона́ підпи́сувала ім’я́м Ле́ся Украї́нка.
paragraphs.source: Lesia Ukrainka was born in 1871 in Volhynia. Her real name was Larysa Kosach, and Lesia was what she was called at home. She signed her poems with the name Lesia Ukrainka.
paragraphs.source_literal: Lesia Ukrainka was-born in thousand eight-hundred seventy first year on Volhynia. In-fact her they-called Larysa Kosach, and by-Lesia her they-called at-home. Own poems she signed by-name Lesia Ukrainka.

paragraphs.target: Її́ ма́ти, Оле́на Пчі́лка, була́ письме́нницею, тому́ вдо́ма бага́то чита́ли й говори́ли украї́нською. Пе́рший вірш, «Наді́я», Ле́ся написа́ла в де́в’ять ро́ків.
paragraphs.source: Her mother, Olena Pchilka, was a writer, so at home they read a lot and spoke Ukrainian. Lesia wrote her first poem, 'Hope', at the age of nine.
paragraphs.source_literal: Her mother, Olena Pchilka, was by-writer, therefore at-home much read and spoke by-Ukrainian. First poem, 'Hope', Lesia wrote in nine of-years.

paragraphs.target: З дити́нства вона́ ду́же хворі́ла, тому́ не ходи́ла до шко́ли, а вивча́ла все вдо́ма. Хво́ра пое́тка ча́сто жила́ в теплі́ших краї́нах: в Іта́лії, в Єги́пті, у Гру́зії.
paragraphs.source: From childhood she was seriously ill, so she did not go to school but studied everything at home. Because of her illness, the poet often lived in warmer countries: in Italy, in Egypt, in Georgia.
paragraphs.source_literal: From childhood she very was-ill, therefore not went to school, and studied everything at-home. Ill poet often lived in warmer countries: in Italy, in Egypt, in Georgia.

paragraphs.target: Хоча́ вона́ була́ хво́ра, вона́ бага́то писа́ла: ві́рші, оповіда́ння, п’є́си. В одному́ ві́рші вона́ пи́ше: «Без наді́ї таки́ сподіва́тись, жи́ти хо́чу!»
paragraphs.source: Although she was ill, she wrote a great deal: poems, short stories, plays. In one poem she writes: 'To go on hoping without hope, I want to live!'
paragraphs.source_literal: Although she was ill, she much wrote: poems, short-stories, plays. In one poem she writes: 'Without hope still to-hope, to-live I-want!'

paragraphs.target: «Лісову́ пі́сню», п’є́су у ві́ршах, вона́ написа́ла в ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т одина́дцятому ро́ці. Це істо́рія лісово́ї ді́вчини Ма́вки, яка́ лю́бить Лука́ша, хло́пця з села́. Але́ Лука́ш не розумі́є її́.
paragraphs.source: She wrote 'The Forest Song', a play in verse, in 1911. It is the story of Mavka, a girl of the forest, who loves Lukash, a young man from the village. But Lukash does not understand her.
paragraphs.source_literal: 'Forest Song', play in verses, she wrote in thousand nine-hundred eleventh year. This story of-forest of-girl of-Mavka, who loves Lukash, of-young-man from village. But Lukash not understands her.

paragraphs.target: Ле́ся Украї́нка поме́рла в ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т трина́дцятому ро́ці в Гру́зії, а похова́ли її́ в Ки́єві. Сього́дні її́ ві́рші вивча́ють у ко́жній шко́лі.
paragraphs.source: Lesia Ukrainka died in 1913 in Georgia, and she was buried in Kyiv. Today her poems are studied in every school.
paragraphs.source_literal: Lesia Ukrainka died in thousand nine-hundred thirteenth year in Georgia, and they-buried her in Kyiv. Today her poems they-study in every school.

questions.explanation: 'Наспра́вді її́ зва́ли Лари́са Ко́сач.' Olena Pchilka was her mother, and Mavka is the heroine of 'The Forest Song'.

questions.explanation: 'Пе́рший вірш, «Наді́я», Ле́ся написа́ла в де́в’ять ро́ків.' The phrase 'в де́в’ять ро́ків' gives a person's age when something happened.

choices: She worked there as a teacher
questions.explanation: 'Хво́ра пое́тка ча́сто жила́ в теплі́ших краї́нах': the poet, who was ill, often lived in warmer countries.

A novel about a village school

exercises.prompt: What are the two meanings of 'во́ля'?
exercises.explanation: 'Во́ля' is freedom, especially of a people, and will, a person's wish or decision. Fate is 'до́ля'.

exercises.explanation: A woman poet is 'пое́тка', and a role after 'була́' takes the instrumental: 'пое́ткою'.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the genitive of 'ві́тер'?
exercises.explanation: The fleeting 'е' drops when an ending is added: 'ві́тру', as in 'Ві́тру нема́є.' 'Ві́тром' is the instrumental and 'ві́трі' the locative.

exercises.hint_source: It is very warm in the steppe in summer.
exercises.explanation: The locative of 'степ' after 'у' is 'степу́', with the ending '-у' and the stress on it. The genitive is 'сте́пу', stressed on the stem.

exercises.hint_source: There is a rhyme in the first line.
exercises.explanation: 'Рядо́к' loses its 'о' in every other form, and the stress moves to the ending: the locative is 'у рядку́'.

choices: The kobzar sang an epic song about fate.
The kobzar told a short story about the steppe.
The kobzar sang an epic song about freedom.

exercises.explanation: 'Дніпро́' takes '-е' in the vocative, and the stress moves to the first syllable: 'Дні́пре'. 'Дніпра́' is the genitive and 'Дніпро́м' the instrumental.

exercises.hint_source: The poet writes: 'My fate, where are you?'
exercises.explanation: The poet speaks to fate, so 'до́ля' is in the vocative: '-я' after a consonant becomes '-е'. The possessive 'моя́' keeps its nominative form.

exercises.prompt_source: This is a poem about freedom.

exercises.prompt: In 'Додо́лу ве́рби гне висо́кі.', which word does 'висо́кі' describe?
exercises.explanation: 'Висо́кі' is a plural adjective, and the only plural noun in the line is 'ве́рби'. The verb stands between them, which poetry allows. In everyday order: 'Ві́тер гне висо́кі ве́рби.'

exercises.hint_source: We read a short story by Ivan Franko.
exercises.explanation: The author follows the work in the genitive. 'Франко́' declines like a masculine noun in '-о': 'Франка́', with the stress on the ending.

exercises.prompt: What is the everyday form of 'я́сная' in 'Ніч яка́ мі́сячна, зо́ряна, я́сная!'?
exercises.explanation: 'Я́сная' is the older uncontracted feminine ending; the modern form is 'я́сна', agreeing with 'ніч', a feminine noun. 'Я́сний' is masculine, and 'я́сно' is neuter.

exercises.prompt_source: Sam read a short story by Franko.

exercises.prompt: Which everyday form does 'завива́' stand for in 'Серди́тий ві́тер завива́'?
exercises.explanation: Poetry often drops the final '-є' of the 'він' form: 'завива́' for 'завива́є', the wind howls. 'Завива́ти' is the infinitive and 'завива́ла' a feminine past.

exercises.prompt: In 'Як умру́, то похова́йте мене́ на моги́лі', what does 'як' mean?
exercises.explanation: Here 'як' means 'when', as it can in speech too: 'Як умру́' is 'Коли́ я помру́'. In the last line of the stanza, 'як реве́ реву́чий', it means 'how'.
A role after 'був' takes the instrumental: 'пое́том'.

exercises.prompt_source: This is a poem by Lesia Ukrainka.
exercises.explanation: The author follows the work in the genitive: 'Ле́ся' becomes 'Ле́сі', and 'Украї́нка' becomes 'Украї́нки'.
The thing liked is the subject of 'подо́батися', and the person is in the dative: literally 'to-me pleases this novel'.
'Нема́є' takes the genitive, and 'ві́тер' loses its 'е' before the ending: 'ві́тру'.

exercises.prompt: Who is spoken to in 'Ду́ми мої́, ду́ми мої́, ли́хо мені́ з ва́ми!'?
exercises.explanation: 'Ду́ми' here means thoughts, and 'ду́ми мої́' is a plural vocative, which has the form of the nominative. The poet speaks to his thoughts as to people.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, which image does Sam like best?
exercises.explanation: 'Мені́ найбі́льше подо́бається о́браз серди́того ві́тру.' 'Серди́того ві́тру' is the genitive after 'о́браз'.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why did Oksana prefer short stories at school?
choices: You can read one in an evening
exercises.explanation: 'Мені́ бі́льше подо́балися оповіда́ння, бо їх мо́жна прочита́ти за оди́н ве́чір.'

exercises.prompt: According to the culture note, who were the kobzars?
choices: Wandering singers, usually blind, who sang dumy to their own playing
exercises.explanation: A kobzar went from village to village and sang to his own playing on the instruments called 'ко́бза' and 'банду́ра'. His great form was the epic song called 'ду́ма'.
